    {
      "startEvent": 657,
      "endEvent": 666,
      "contextStartEvent": 628,
      "contextEndEvent": 700,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "They are in fact wounded theists.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "yes",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "high",
      "explanation": "The label converts reported loss of belief into continued belief motivated by revenge (E660–666). Shermer's disappointment supplies a biographical trigger, but not evidence of concealed theism. A limits this to 'many cases' and includes Christians as wounded too (E667–686); whether this explicitly neutralizes objections regardless of merit remains unclear."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 784,
      "endEvent": 827,
      "contextStartEvent": 741,
      "contextEndEvent": 833,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "your knowledge is local. My knowledge is divine.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["shame"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "Human ignorance legitimately does not entail absence of a reason (E792–799). However, the divine perspective and ant analogy might insulate design from adverse evidence without establishing a justifying reason. Calling criticism arrogant adds pressure (E808–815), but A expressly endorses inquiry and human reason at E828–833, preventing a confident protection finding."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1623,
      "endEvent": 1632,
      "contextStartEvent": 1596,
      "contextEndEvent": 1669,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the small gaggle of public atheists",
      "form": "no",
      "substitution": "no",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity", "ridicule"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "A discounts named dissenters through their public atheist identity, potentially restricting admissible scientific disagreement by affiliation (E1623–1629). Yet he also gives substantive readings of Stenger and Krauss (E1615–1622). This is an argument about expert disagreement, not a settled catchphrase; whether identity independently disqualifies their objections is unclear."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 2048,
      "endEvent": 2056,
      "contextStartEvent": 2036,
      "contextEndEvent": 2131,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "the New Testament is in the old concealed the Old Testament is in the new revealed.",
      "form": "yes",
      "substitution": "unclear",
      "protection": "unclear",
      "emotionalDevices": ["identity"],
      "confidence": "medium",
      "explanation": "The maxim establishes an exclusive interpretive lens before A reinterprets Pharaoh's hardened heart (E2063–2071), without a passage-specific reason for that reading. Later, Jesus's temple language supports metaphor generally (E2097–2111), and A allows literal and metaphorical readings together (E2125–2131). Whether the maxim replaces interpretation or immunizes free will remains uncertain."
    }
  ],
  "contrasts": [
    {
      "startEvent": 1335,
      "endEvent": 1351,
      "speaker": "A",
      "quote": "Notice that Jesus heals the blind man, but he doesn't heal blindness.",
      "explanation": "The memorable distinction summarizes a supported limitation: biblical intervention is selective. A points to continuing Israelite suffering and lamenting Psalms, then explains spiritual purposes at E1352–1373. It does not by itself explain every nonintervention, but it earns its narrower conclusion."
    },
    {
      "startEvent": 1794,
      "endEvent": 1817,
      "speaker": "B",
      "quote": "that doesn't make their belief true, the fact that they find solace in it.",
      "explanation": "B explicitly grants suffering believers' comfort before distinguishing comfort from evidence of truth. The preceding oncologist analogy (E1783–1793) explains why firsthand suffering need not confer explanatory expertise. He does not infer that a comforting belief must therefore be false."
    }
